Chesterfield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north-east Derbyshire
s1loc: Chesterfield builds its visitor economy around the Crooked Spire of the Church of St Mary and All Saints, the twisted 228-foot landmark whose tower tours draw visitors from across the country. The Chesterfield Museum in the neo-Gothic Stephenson Memorial Hall, the vast open-air Chesterfield Market with its 200-plus stalls, and the restored Chesterfield Canal, the old Cuckoo Dyke, give the town a strong historic core throughout the year.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Victorian Queen's Park, with its boating lake, miniature railway and cricket ground, and reaches out to Poolsbrook Country Park and Holmebrook Valley Park. As a gateway to the Peak District, the town feeds walkers and cyclists towards the moors and trails, while local activity operators and the Healthy Living Centre keep families busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run from the Pomegranate Theatre, one of the oldest in the country, and the adjoining Winding Wheel, out to nearby Bolsover Castle, the Cavendish family's Stuart show mansion, and Hardwick Hall. Renishaw Hall and Gardens, the historic Shambles quarter and a busy market-town events calendar add to the seasonal draw across this corner of Derbyshire.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn base across the town centre and the A61 corridor, plus a guiding scene working the Crooked Spire and the Peak District day trips. Chesterfield station on the Midland Main Line brings visitors in fast, with Chatsworth House, the Peak District National Park and the Derbyshire dales all a short hop for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.

Ashford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Ashford and mid-Kent
s1loc: Ashford anchors a busy mid-Kent visitor economy around the Ashford Designer Outlet, a major draw with around 100 stores and a clutch of restaurants pulling shoppers from across the region. The historic St Mary's Church and the old town centre, the County Square shopping quarter and the town's position as an international gateway give Ashford steady year-round footfall across this corner of Kent.

The leisure and activity layer is led by the Eureka Leisure Park, home to the Cineworld Ashford multiplex, restaurants and a health club, alongside the Stour Centre and the Julie Rose Stadium athletics track. The Conningbrook Lakes Country Park and Singleton Lake give families watersports and walking, while the surrounding Kent Downs Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty feeds walkers and cyclists through the season.

Heritage and culture take in the Ashford Borough Museum, the medieval church quarter and the Godinton House and Gardens estate just outside the town, with the historic market town of Tenterden and the Kent and East Sussex Railway a short drive away. The Revelation arts venue and a town events calendar add to the cultural mix across spring and summer.

Underpinning it all is a strong hotel base around the Eureka park and the M20, plus a tour-operator scene built on Ashford's role as a Eurostar gateway. Ashford International station on the high-speed line and the Eurostar route bring domestic and continental visitors in, with the Kent Downs, Canterbury and the coast all an easy day trip for the surrounding area's seasonal draw.

Guildford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Guildford and west Surrey
s1loc: Guildford anchors a busy Surrey visitor economy around the Norman Guildford Castle, whose Great Tower offers panoramic views over the town, and Guildford Cathedral, one of only two Anglican cathedrals built in Britain since the Reformation. The cobbled High Street with its Guildhall clock, the Guildford Museum and Guildford House Gallery, and the riverside walks along the River Wey draw steady year-round footfall.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the Castle Grounds and Stoke Park out to the River Wey Navigation, where Guildford Boat House runs trips and hire along the towpath. The Spectrum Leisure Centre, Guildford Lido and the surrounding Surrey Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, with St Martha's Hill and the North Downs Way, keep families and activity operators working hard through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Yvonne Arnaud Theatre beside the river and the G Live arts and music venue, which carry the events calendar with theatre, comedy and the town's Christmas pantomime. The Guildford House Gallery, the Watts Gallery at Compton and the Loseley Park estate, plus the GuilFest legacy and a busy festival programme, add to the cultural draw across the year.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel base across the town centre and the A3 corridor, plus a guiding and tour scene built on the castle, cathedral and Surrey Hills day trips. Guildford station on the main line to London Waterloo brings commuters and visitors in fast, with Godalming, Farnham and the wider North Downs all close for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.

Lewisham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south-east London
s1loc: Lewisham anchors a south-east London visitor economy around the Horniman Museum and Gardens at Forest Hill, the gift of tea trader Frederick Horniman, with its 350,000-object collection, acclaimed aquarium and 16 acres of gardens overlooking the city. The historic heath at Blackheath, the Deptford waterfront and the borough's many green-flag parks give the area a strong draw across the year.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Beckenham Place Park, home to London's first purpose-built open-water swimming lake, with watersports, lessons and woodland trails across the borough's largest green space. Ladywell Fields, Manor House Gardens and the Glass Mill Leisure Centre keep families and activity operators busy, while the heath at Blackheath hosts kite-flying, fairs and seasonal events.

Heritage and culture run deep, from Deptford Dockyard, founded in 1513 as a Royal Navy yard, and the Christopher Marlowe story, out to The Albany performing-arts centre and the artist-run Lewisham Arthouse. Deptford Market, the historic streets of Blackheath Village and Brockley, and a busy programme of festivals and events add to the cultural mix across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guesthouse base across the borough and a guiding scene built on the Deptford naval story and the Horniman draw. Lewisham, Blackheath and Forest Hill stations, the DLR and frequent links into central London bring visitors in fast, with Greenwich, Eltham Palace and the Thames riverside all close for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.

Woolwich.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of riverside south-east London
s1loc: Woolwich builds its visitor economy around the Royal Arsenal, the historic armaments quarter on the south bank of the Thames that once employed close to 80,000 people and now houses one of London's biggest concentrations of listed buildings. The riverside walk, the Royal Arsenal Pier with its Thames Clipper service, and the regenerated waterfront give Woolwich a striking historic core across the year.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the Thames riverside path and the Woolwich Ferry across to nearby green spaces, with watersports and river trips working the estuary. Plumstead Common, the leisure facilities around General Gordon Square and the indoor activity venues clustered in the regenerated Arsenal quarter keep families and operators busy through the warmer season along this stretch of the river.

Heritage and culture centre on Woolwich Works, the major cultural district opened in 2021 in the Arsenal's historic buildings, with a 1,200-seat auditorium, performance courtyard and resident companies. The Royal Artillery heritage, the listed Grade I and II buildings of the West site and a growing events calendar of concerts and festivals add to the cultural draw across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a rapidly growing hotel base around the Arsenal and a guiding scene built on the town's military and riverside story. The Woolwich Elizabeth line station, opened in 2022, plus Woolwich Arsenal rail and DLR and the ferry, bring visitors in fast, with Greenwich, Eltham Palace and the O2 riverside all close for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.

Weston-super-Mare.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Somerset coast
s1loc: Weston-super-Mare anchors a traditional Somerset seaside visitor economy around the Grand Pier, dubbed the West Country's favourite attraction, with its go-karts, simulators, arcades and fairground rides under one roof. The huge sandy beach with its famous summer donkey rides, the Marine Parade seafront and the landmark Tropicana on the front draw holidaymakers and day-trippers along this stretch of coast across the season.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the seafront amusements out to the SeaQuarium and the glow-in-the-dark mini-golf near the Tropicana, with the Helicopter Museum, the world's largest, just outside the town. Beach watersports, the Sand Sculpture Festival, the Puxton Park family attraction and the winter ice rink keep operators busy, while Brean Down and the coast path feed walkers through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture take in the Weston Museum and the Clara's Cottage Victorian display, the SeaQuarium quarter and the seafront's Banksy connection, with the Tropicana the setting for the artist's 2015 Dismaland show. The Playhouse Theatre, The Blakehay Theatre and a busy programme of festivals, including the air festival and sand art, add to the cultural draw across spring and summer.

Underpinning it all is one of the region's deepest seaside hotel and guesthouse bases along the seafront and Beach Road, plus a tour and coach-operator scene built on the traditional resort trade. Weston-super-Mare station on the main line and the nearby M5 bring visitors in fast, with Clevedon, Burnham-on-Sea and the Mendip Hills all close for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.

West Bromwich.region: West Bromwich and the Black Country
West Bromwich.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Black Country
s1loc: West Bromwich anchors a Black Country visitor economy around The Hawthorns, home of West Bromwich Albion since 1878 and a 26,000-plus all-seater stadium that draws match-day and tour crowds. The Oak House, a striking timber-framed yeoman's house dating from the 1620s with its later belvedere tower, and the town's industrial heritage give West Bromwich a strong historic core across the year.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Sandwell Valley Country Park, an 1,800-acre green space with woodlands, pools, a sailing club, a mountain-bike trail, an adventure playground and the RSPB visitor centre. Dartmouth Park, the restored Victorian Sandwell Valley Visitor Centre with its walled kitchen garden, and indoor activity venues keep families and operators busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run from the Oak House museum and Sandwell Priory ruins out to the wider Black Country story, with the Public arts legacy and a busy events calendar in the town centre. Nearby Sandwell Park Farm, the canal network and the Black Country Living Museum a short drive away add to the cultural draw across this part of the West Midlands through the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base along the A41 and the wider Sandwell corridor, plus a guiding scene built on the football and industrial-heritage story. The West Bromwich Central Metro tram, the nearby M5 and frequent links into Birmingham bring visitors in fast, with Wednesbury, Smethwick and the canalside attractions all close for the surrounding area's seasonal pull.
